checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template with Starter Content, or create one. Open a level that has a Landscape, or create a new level and make a Landscape in Landscape Mode. Decide where the main route runs across it and where a combat space is, and mark both with a few cubes. Open Edit > Editor Preferences, go to the Experimental section, and enable Procedural Foliage.
Create a Procedural Foliage Spawner asset named PFS_Forest. Place it over the landscape and scale it so that it covers the play area.

Create two Static Mesh Foliage assets named FT_Tree_A and FT_Tree_B and give each one a mesh. If you have no tree meshes, the bush from the Starter Content and a tall cone can stand in for two kinds of tree. Add both to the Foliage Types array of PFS_Forest.
On FT_Tree_A, set Num Steps to 3, Initial Seed Density to 0.25 and Shade Radius to 50. On FT_Tree_B, set Overlap Priority to 1 and enable Spawns in Shade.
For both types, enable Align to Normal and Random Yaw under Placement. Then click Resimulate on the spawner to grow the forest.
Place one Procedural Foliage Blocking Volume over the main route and one over the combat space. Click Resimulate again.
Walk the route in PIE. Note any tree that still blocks a view the player needs, and fix it with the blocking volume.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Enable the Geometry Script plugin and restart the editor.
Create a Blueprint named BP_Tool_Ramp with GeneratedDynamicMeshActor as its parent class. Add the Instance Editable variables Width, Length, Height and Steps.
In the event Event On Rebuild Generated Mesh, append boxes that use the variables, so that the actor builds a ramp or a stair block. If you need a temporary mesh, use Request and Release Mesh for it.

Place three BP_Tool_Ramp actors in the level. Change their variables in the Details panel so that each one fits the character in a different way: a ramp that the character can walk up, a stair whose steps are lower than 45 cm, and a tall block that the character can only reach with a jump. Test them in PIE.

Add an event named Bake with Call In Editor turned on. It copies the dynamic mesh to a Static Mesh asset. The Geometry Script library has two functions for this: Create New Static Mesh Asset from Mesh makes a new asset at the path you give it, for example /Game/Blockout/SM_Ramp_Baked, and Copy Mesh to Static Mesh writes into an asset that already exists. Use the first one the first time.
Replace one ramp with a Static Mesh Actor that uses the baked asset. Move the tool actor below the level and keep it there as the template.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one, and work in any level with a floor. Enter Modeling Mode by pressing Shift+5. In the Create category, make a Box column with a size that suits a character, for example 100 x 100 x 400.
Select the column. In the Xform category, open Pattern and tile the column along a Line, so that you get a row of 8 columns along a route.
Make a floor tile and use Pattern in Grid mode to build a plaza of 6 x 6 tiles.
Make a short pillar and use Pattern in Circle mode to put a ring of pillars around an arena. Move the pattern plane to set the position of the ring.
Use Duplicate on one column and edit the copy. Then use Merge to combine the ring pillars into one mesh.
Run Bake Transform on the merged mesh, and then use Convert to turn it into a Static Mesh. Walk across the plaza in PIE.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a level that has a Landscape with Edit Layers enabled, or create one: make a new level, enter Landscape Mode, choose New on the Manage tab, and check Enable Edit Layers. Sculpt a few dips and hills, and place a tall cube as a landmark. In Landscape Mode, open the Edit Layer stack and add a new Spline Edit Layer. The splines need this layer to change the terrain.
Open the Manage tab and select the Spline tool. Hold Ctrl and click to lay a road from a start area to the landmark. Use Alt+drag to extend it.
Select all control points. Set Half-Width to the width of your road, and set Side Falloff so that the edges blend into the terrain. Set Layer Name to a paint layer named Road.
On the segments that cross a dip in the ground, enable Raise Terrain. On one other segment, disable it and compare the two results.

Make a road mesh: in Modeling Mode, create a long flat Box, accept it as a Static Mesh, and name the asset SM_RoadSection. Select the spline segments and add a Spline Mesh that uses SM_RoadSection. Enable Scale to Width and choose the correct Forward Axis.
Select a control point and use the scale tool to drag its tangents until the curve is smooth. Press End to snap the points to the landscape.
Walk or drive along the road in PIE. Check that the raised sides of the road do not block the view of the landmark.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In a test level with a floor and a NavMeshBoundsVolume, place three Nav Modifier Volumes side by side as lanes. Scale each one to about X=2, Y=6, Z=1.
Create three Blueprints with the parent class Nav Area: BP_Area_Neutral, BP_Area_Lane1 and BP_Area_Lane2. Give Lane1 a blue Draw Color and Lane2 a red Draw Color.
Assign one Area Class to each volume. Press P and check that the lanes show in their Draw Colors on the NavMesh.

Create two Blueprints with the parent class Navigation Query Filter: BP_QueryFilter1 and BP_QueryFilter2. In each one, add the three Area Classes and use Travel Cost Override with a value of 100, so that a different lane is cheap in each filter.

Make an AI walker: duplicate BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, delete its input nodes, and on Begin Play call AI Move To toward a target sphere that you place on the far side of the lanes. Add an Instance Editable variable for the Filter Class pin of the node. Place two walkers. Set Filter Class to BP_QueryFilter1 on one walker and to BP_QueryFilter2 on the other.
Click Simulate. Confirm that each walker takes a different lane to the same target.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Work in a level with a large floor and a NavMeshBoundsVolume that covers it. Select the RecastNavMesh-Default actor and enable Draw Tile Build Times. Press P to see the NavMesh and the build time of each tile.
Place a Nav Modifier Volume over an open area that covers several tiles. Set its Nav Mesh Resolution to Low. Compare the build times inside and outside the volume.
Build a tight area from three cube obstacles with small gaps between them. Cover it with a second Nav Modifier Volume and set that one to High.
On the RecastNavMesh actor, enable Draw Tile Resolutions and Draw Tile Build Times Heat Map. Check that the colors match your zones.
Make BP_NavResCarrier, an Actor Blueprint with a NavModifier component that is set to Low. Drag it across the NavMesh and watch the tiles rebuild.
Open Project Settings, go to Navigation Mesh, then Generation, and find Nav Mesh Resolution Params. Note the Cell Size of each resolution.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Use a level with a floor, a NavMeshBoundsVolume and one AI walker that moves between two spheres. To make the walker, duplicate BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, delete its input nodes, and add logic that calls AI Move To toward one sphere and, on success, toward the other, again and again. Open Project Settings, go to Navigation Mesh, then Runtime, and set Runtime Generation to Dynamic Modifiers Only.

Create an Actor Blueprint named BP_RotatingGate with a Cube (scale about X=4, Y=1.5, Z=1) and a Rotating Movement component. Place it on the route of the walker and click Simulate. Notice that the NavMesh does not change yet.
Add a Nav Modifier component to BP_RotatingGate. Simulate again and watch the NavMesh update as the gate turns. The tiles that are being updated are shown in red.
Create an Actor Blueprint named BP_SlidingBlock with a Sphere that moves back and forth. Drive it with a Timeline that uses Set Relative Location and a Lerp on X over a distance of about 1000.
Simulate with Dynamic Modifiers Only. Then switch Runtime Generation to Dynamic and Simulate again. Compare how the NavMesh reacts to BP_SlidingBlock in each mode.
Set the mode back to the one that your level really needs, and write down why.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Make a flat test level with a Floor scaled to 10x10 and a NavMeshBoundsVolume. Place two Sphere actors as targets on opposite sides.

Copy BP_ThirdPersonCharacter and name the copy BP_NPC_NoAvoidance. Remove the input nodes. Add an Instance Editable Actor variable named Target, and on Begin Play call AI Move To with Pawn set to self and Target Actor set to Target.
Place two groups of 4 to 6 NPCs that face each other across the level. Each group targets the sphere on the far side. Click Simulate and watch them collide in the middle.
Duplicate the Blueprint and name it BP_NPC_RVO. On the Character Movement component, under Avoidance, enable Use RVOAvoidance and set Avoidance Consideration Radius to 100. Test the same crossing.
Duplicate the Blueprint again and name it BP_NPC_DetourCrowd. Set its AI Controller Class to DetourCrowdAIController. Test the same crossing.
Open Project Settings, go to Crowd Manager, and note the values of Max Agents and Max Agent Radius. Change one value and observe the effect.

quiz.q: Pathfinding already routes around walls. Why does the guide say you still need avoidance?
choices: Pathfinding is only for players
Avoidance handles moving obstacles and other agents; pathfinding handles objects that do not move
Avoidance replaces the NavMesh
Pathfinding does not work with Characters
quiz.explain: Pathfinding finds a path around static objects. Avoidance algorithms are better for moving obstacles and other agents.

quiz.q: Where does RVO avoidance live in Unreal?
choices: In the Character Movement component of the Character class
In the AI Controller
In the RecastNavMesh actor
In the Blackboard
quiz.explain: RVO is included in the Character Movement component. The guide enables Use RVOAvoidance there.

quiz.q: Which is a real limitation of RVO listed by the guide?
choices: It needs a Behavior Tree
It has a fixed maximum number of agents
It does not use the NavMesh, so agents can go out of bounds
It only works on Pawns that are not Characters
quiz.explain: RVO does not use the Navigation Mesh for avoidance. Agents can potentially leave the navigable area. It is also less configurable and limited to the Character class.

quiz.q: How do you turn on Detour Crowd avoidance for an agent Blueprint?
choices: Enable Use RVOAvoidance
Set AI Controller Class to DetourCrowdAIController
Add a Nav Modifier component
Increase Avoidance Consideration Radius
quiz.explain: The guide sets the AI Controller Class to DetourCrowdAIController. Detour Crowd can be used with any Pawn class.

quiz.q: What is a limitation of the Detour Crowd Manager?
choices: It only works with the Character class
It has a fixed maximum number of agents set in Project Settings
It cannot avoid other agents
It disables pathfinding
quiz.explain: Detour Crowd has a fixed Max Agents value, set in Project Settings under Crowd Manager.

quiz.q: Can you run RVO and Detour Crowd together in one project?
choices: Yes, they combine for better results
Yes, but only in packaged builds
No; the guide says they should be used exclusively
Only if Max Agents is above 100
quiz.explain: Both systems work independently and should be used exclusively in your project.

quiz.q: Why does the guide say Detour Crowd gives better avoidance quality than plain RVO?
choices: It uses adaptive RVO sampling biased toward the agent's direction, plus path corridor optimizations
It runs at a higher tick rate
It uses the GPU
It teleports blocked agents
quiz.explain: Detour Crowd samples velocities adaptively with a bias toward the agent's direction and adds visibility and topology path corridor optimizations.

quiz.q: Which two Crowd Manager settings does the guide name?
choices: Sight Radius and Hearing Range
Max Agents and Max Agent Radius
Cell Size and Tile Size
Walk Speed and Acceleration
quiz.explain: In Project Settings > Crowd Manager you can adjust Max Agents and the Max Agent Radius used for the avoidance calculation.

LDQ109.done_when: Send a screenshot of BT_Enemy taken while playing, with the active branch highlighted. Also send a short video clip (30 seconds or less) or a second screenshot that shows the enemy chasing you after it sees you.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create a folder named AI. In it, make Enemy_Character (a copy of BP_ThirdPersonCharacter with its script removed and Max Walk Speed set to 120) and Enemy_Controller (an AIController Blueprint). Set the AI Controller Class on Enemy_Character to Enemy_Controller.
Create a Blackboard named BB_Enemy with three keys: EnemyActor (type Object with base class Actor), HasLineOfSight (type Bool) and PatrolLocation (type Vector).

Create a Behavior Tree named BT_Enemy. Under the Root, add a Selector named AI Root. Under it, add a Sequence named Chase Player on the left, a Sequence named Patrol in the middle, and a Wait node of 1.0 on the right.

Make a task named BTT_FindRandomPatrol. From Event Receive Execute AI, call GetRandomReachablePointInRadius with a radius of 1000, then Set Blackboard Value as Vector for PatrolLocation, then Finish Execute. Under Patrol, add this task, then Move To PatrolLocation, then Wait 4.0 with Random Deviation 1.0.

Under Chase Player, add Rotate to Face BBEntry (set to EnemyActor), then BTT_ChasePlayer (a task that sets the walk speed to 500 through a function on the character), then Move To EnemyActor. Add a Blackboard decorator on Chase Player with the key HasLineOfSight and Observer aborts set to Both.

In Enemy_Controller, connect Event On Possess to Run Behavior Tree. Add an AIPerception component with an AI Sight config and turn on Detect Neutrals. On Target Perception Updated, set the Blackboard keys for actors that have the tag Player, and start a timer of 4 s that clears the keys when sight is lost.
Add the tag Player to the player character, place a NavMeshBoundsVolume, and play. Watch the tree switch branches in the Behavior Tree editor.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Work in a level with a floor, a NavMeshBoundsVolume and a few cubes as cover. Enable the Environment Query Editor plugin if it is not enabled yet. Create EQC_PlayerContext with the parent class EnvQueryContext_BlueprintBase, and override Provide Single Actor so that it returns Get Player Character.

Create an Environment Query named EQS_SpawnPoint. Add a Points: Donut generator around EQC_PlayerContext with Inner Radius 800, Outer Radius 1600 and 3 rings. Keep Projection Data on, so that the points land on the NavMesh.

Add a Trace test with Test Purpose set to Filter Only and Context set to EQC_PlayerContext. The guide disables Bool Match to keep the points that can see the player. Flip it and compare, so that you keep the hidden points for spawns. Also add a Pathfinding test with Path Exist and Skip Unreachable.
Add a Distance test set to Score Only with a Scoring Factor of -1.0, so that hidden points that are closer get a higher score.

Create BP_EQSTestPawn from the EQS Testing Pawn class, set its Query Template to EQS_SpawnPoint, and place it in the level. Move the cover cubes until the Winner, the point with the best score, is where you want a spawn.
Optional: in a small Behavior Tree, use Run EQSQuery to write the result to a Vector key, and then use Move To to go there.
